description: Hajj rituals, the meaning of Zakah and Khums, Nisab, and fasting during Ramadan.
content_html:
Hajj: The Pilgrimage to Mecca

Hajj is the annual pilgrimage to the holy city of Mecca. It is obligatory — at least once in a lifetime — for every Muslim who is physically able and financially able to make the journey. Those who are too ill, too poor, or who have dependants who cannot be cared for in their absence are exempt. The pilgrimage takes place during the Islamic month of Dhul Hijjah. The Qur’an refers to Hajj and connects it to the Prophet Ibrahim: “And proclaim to the people the Hajj [pilgrimage]; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every distant pass” (Surah 22:27, al-Hajj).

Key Fact

Hajj commemorates the trials of the Prophet Ibrahim — his willingness to sacrifice his son Isma’il and the actions of his wife Hajar. The pilgrimage re-enacts key moments: wearing ihram, circling the Ka’bah, walking between Safa and Marwa, standing at Arafat, and the symbolic stoning of the devil at Mina.

The Rituals of Hajj

Before entering Mecca, pilgrims put on ihram. Men wear two white unstitched cloths; women wear modest clothing. This signals entry into a sacred state where arguing, cutting hair and certain other activities are forbidden. The white garments also represent equality — all pilgrims look the same regardless of wealth or social status.

Once in Mecca, pilgrims perform tawaf — circling the Ka’bah seven times in an anti-clockwise direction. They then walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, re-enacting Hajar’s search for water for her son Isma’il. The pilgrimage culminates in the wuquf at Arafat, where pilgrims stand together in prayer and reflection — the spiritual heart of Hajj. The ritual stoning at Mina symbolises rejecting the devil’s temptations, as Ibrahim did. Hajj concludes with the festival of Eid-ul-Adha, during which an animal is sacrificed and the meat shared among family, neighbours and those in need.

For the individual pilgrim, Hajj is a chance to seek forgiveness for past sins and to stand before Allah with a ‘clean slate’. Many Muslims say that returning from Hajj feels like being reborn. On a communal level, Hajj brings together Muslims from every nation, ethnicity and culture — up to two million pilgrims at a time — and makes real the unity of the global Muslim community (the ummah). The identical white ihram reinforces that no Muslim is superior to another before Allah. Muslims who have completed the pilgrimage may use the title Hajji (male) or Hajjah (female) as a mark of respect within their communities.

Zakah: Compulsory Almsgiving

Zakah is the third Pillar of Sunni Islam and one of the Ten Obligatory Acts for Shi’a Muslims. It is a compulsory annual payment of 2.5% on savings that have been held for a full lunar year and exceed the minimum threshold known as the Nisab. Zakah is not seen as charity in the Western sense — it is a religious obligation, a purification of wealth, and a reminder that all wealth ultimately belongs to Allah.

The Qur’an specifies eight categories of people who may receive Zakah, including the poor, the indebted and travellers in need (Surah 9:60, at-Tawbah). Beyond compulsory Zakah, Muslims are encouraged to give Sadaqah — voluntary almsgiving at any time and in any amount. Sadaqah can include acts of kindness, not only money. The Qur’an instructs: “They ask you, [O Muhammad], what they should spend. Say, ‘Whatever you spend of good is [to be] for parents and relatives and orphans and the needy and the traveller’” (Surah 2:215, al-Baqarah).

Key Fact

Zakah is set at 2.5% of eligible savings held above the Nisab threshold for one lunar year. It is a religious duty and purification of wealth — not charity. Sadaqah is voluntary and can be given in any form at any time.

Khums: The Shi’a Additional Obligation

Khums means ‘one fifth’ in Arabic. It is a Shi’a religious tax of 20% on certain categories of income and profit — including business profits, treasure troves, lawfully gained minerals and surplus income — paid after all basic living needs are met. Half goes to the descendants of the Prophet (sayyids) who are in need; the other half goes to the Imam (or, during the Major Occultation, to his authorised representatives). Khums is distinct from and additional to Zakah. It reflects the Shi’a theological emphasis on the Imams as rightful leaders of the Muslim community.

Sawm: Fasting in Ramadan

Sawm is the obligatory fast during Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. Muslims abstain from eating, drinking, smoking and sexual relations from dawn (Fajr) until sunset (Maghrib) each day for the entire month. Fasting is not just about hunger — it is an act of obedience, self-discipline and empathy with those who go without. The Qur’an commands: “O you who have believed, decreed upon you is fasting as it was decreed upon those before you that you may become righteous” (Surah 2:183, al-Baqarah).

Certain groups are exempt from fasting: children, the elderly, pregnant or nursing women, travellers and those who are seriously ill. People who miss fasts must make them up later, or in some cases pay a fidyah — a compensatory feeding of a poor person for each day missed.

Ramadan is particularly sacred because it is the month in which the Qur’an was first revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Jibril. Within Ramadan, the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) occurs in the last ten days, most likely on one of the odd-numbered nights. The Qur’an describes it as better than a thousand months. Muslims spend this night in extended prayer, Qur’an recitation and supplication. Many Muslims, particularly men, retreat to the mosque for the last ten days of Ramadan in a practice called i’tikaf. The month ends with the festival of Eid-ul-Fitr, a joyful celebration of the community having fasted and worshipped together.
exam_tip_html: Examiners frequently ask students to ‘Explain’ the significance of Hajj or Zakah — make sure you cover both what Muslims do and why it matters spiritually and communally. When writing about Zakah, always specify the 2.5% rate and the Nisab threshold; students who write ‘Muslims give money to the poor’ without these details are working at a low level. For the 15-mark Discuss question, you might be asked whether Hajj or Zakah is the most important Pillar — in that case, compare the individual and community dimensions of each and give a reasoned conclusion. Distinguish clearly between Zakah (Sunni and Shi’a) and Khums (Shi’a only). Accurate spelling of Nisab, Sadaqah, Laylat al-Qadr and ihram is rewarded on extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hajj is an obligatory once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage to Mecca for able Muslims, involving ihram, tawaf, standing at Arafat, the stoning at Mina and ending with Eid-ul-Adha; it commemorates the trials of Ibrahim and unifies the global Muslim community.
  • Zakah (2.5% of savings above the Nisab) is a compulsory religious duty that purifies wealth; Sadaqah is voluntary additional giving. Khums (20% of certain surplus earnings) is an additional Shi’a obligation distinct from Zakah.
  • Sawm means fasting throughout Ramadan — the month the Qur’an was revealed — from dawn to sunset. The Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in the last ten days is considered the most blessed night of the year.

practice_questions.text: State what Muslims must wear when entering the state of ihram during Hajj.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for: two white unstitched cloths (for men) / plain white garments / seamless white cloth. Accept: simple white clothing symbolising equality before Allah. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims do on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr).
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for any two of the following: they spend the night in extended prayer / recitation of the Qur'an / supplication (du'a) / some observe i'tikaf (retreat to the mosque for the last ten days of Ramadan) / they seek blessings on the night the Qur'an was first revealed. [2 marks — 1 per valid point]

practice_questions.text: Outline why the pilgrimage of Hajj is important for Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for a developed outline including: it is an obligatory Pillar for those who are able / it commemorates the trials of Ibrahim and his family / it symbolises equality before Allah (ihram) / it unites the global Muslim community (ummah) / it gives the individual an opportunity to seek forgiveness and spiritual renewal / it re-enacts key events connected to the origins of Islam. Award three marks for at least two of these points developed clearly. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Zakah is important for Muslims.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Zakah purifies a Muslim's wealth by acknowledging that all wealth belongs to Allah. Giving 2.5% of savings above the Nisab reminds Muslims that money is a trust from Allah and not something to be hoarded selfishly.
• Zakah reduces inequality and supports those in need — the Qur'an specifies eight categories of recipients including the poor, the indebted and travellers (Surah 9:60). This promotes social justice, a key Islamic value.
• Zakah strengthens community bonds by redistributing wealth to those who need it, reflecting the Muslim concept of ummah (global community).
• It is a divine command and one of the Five Pillars, so fulfilling it is an act of obedience to Allah.
Mastering: Two developed points each with a named source, clear explanation of significance.
Secure: Two developed points, at least one source.
Developing: Two basic points, limited sources or development.
Emerging: One point, brief. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Sawm (fasting) is the most spiritually demanding of the Five Pillars.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Sawm requires physical self-denial for an entire month — no food, drink or other physical pleasures from dawn to sunset — which demands extraordinary willpower and discipline.
• Fasting is an internal, invisible act that only Allah can see, making it a particularly sincere demonstration of submission. The Qur'an says it is decreed so that Muslims 'may become righteous' (Surah 2:183).
• The Night of Power within Ramadan is described as better than a thousand months, giving Sawm an unparalleled spiritual intensity.
• Fasting cultivates empathy with the poor and gratitude for Allah's blessings.

Arguments against:
• Hajj could be argued to be more demanding because it requires financial sacrifice, long travel, physical endurance and the performance of many rituals over several days. For many Muslims, it is a once-in-a-lifetime transformation.
• Salah is performed five times every single day of a Muslim's life, which could be seen as a more constant and pervasive spiritual discipline than a month of fasting.
• Zakah involves giving up real wealth permanently, which may be the hardest demand for those with limited means.
• The most spiritually demanding act is subjective and may depend on the individual Muslim's circumstances and strengths.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named Qur'anic references, explicit comparison of the Pillars, explicit weighing of arguments and a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed, at least one source, clear conclusion.
Developing: Both sides but limited development or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided, brief, minimal sources. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between Zakah and Khums.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for: Zakah is obligatory for both Sunni and Shi'a Muslims / set at 2.5% of savings above the Nisab / paid annually on eligible wealth. Khums is a Shi'a-only obligation / set at 20% (one fifth) of certain surplus earnings / paid to the Imam or his representatives. Award three marks for a developed contrast that clearly identifies both obligations and notes the Sunni/Shi'a distinction. [3 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What percentage of savings above the Nisab must Muslims pay as Zakah each year?
Which of the following best describes the significance of Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power)?
options: The night on which Muhammad was born
The night on which the Qur'an was first revealed to Muhammad
The night on which Ibrahim was commanded to sacrifice his son

knowledge_checks.q: The minimum threshold of wealth above which Zakah becomes obligatory is called the _____.
The state of ritual purity and the white seamless garment worn during Hajj is called _____.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: Compulsory 2.5% tax on savings above the Nisab
Shi'a 20% tax on certain surplus earnings

flashcard_questions.q: What is Hajj and when does it take place?
flashcard_questions.a: The annual pilgrimage to Mecca; it takes place during the Islamic month of Dhul Hijjah.
The state of ritual purity; men wear two white seamless cloths symbolising equality before Allah.

flashcard_questions.q: What ritual do pilgrims perform when they first arrive at the Ka'bah?
flashcard_questions.a: Tawaf — circling the Ka'bah seven times in an anti-clockwise direction.

flashcard_questions.q: Which moment is considered the spiritual heart of Hajj?
flashcard_questions.a: The wuquf — standing together on the plain of Arafat in prayer and reflection.

flashcard_questions.q: What festival marks the end of Hajj?
flashcard_questions.a: Eid-ul-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifice, commemorating Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice Isma'il.
Compulsory annual almsgiving of 2.5% of savings above the Nisab threshold.
The minimum wealth threshold above which Zakah becomes obligatory.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Sadaqah differ from Zakah?
flashcard_questions.a: Sadaqah is voluntary giving at any time; Zakah is a compulsory religious duty.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Khums and which Muslims pay it?
flashcard_questions.a: A Shi'a obligation to give 20% of certain surplus earnings; Shi'a Muslims only.
Fasting from dawn to sunset throughout Ramadan — the fourth Pillar of Sunni Islam.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Ramadan considered the holiest month in Islam?
flashcard_questions.a: It is the month in which the Qur'an was first revealed to the Prophet Muhammad.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr)?
flashcard_questions.a: A night in the last ten days of Ramadan when the Qur'an was first revealed; described as better than a thousand months.

glossary_terms.definition: The annual pilgrimage to Mecca in Saudi Arabia, obligatory for every Muslim who is physically and financially able; the fifth Pillar of Sunni Islam.
The state of ritual purity and the white, seamless garment worn by pilgrims during Hajj, symbolising equality before Allah.
The Festival of Sacrifice, marking the end of Hajj and commemorating Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son Isma'il.
The compulsory annual almsgiving paid by Muslims on savings above the Nisab threshold, set at 2.5% of eligible wealth.
The minimum amount of wealth a Muslim must possess before Zakah becomes obligatory; often calculated as the equivalent of 85 grams of gold.
Voluntary charitable giving in Islam, given above and beyond the obligatory Zakah.
A Shi'a Islamic obligation to donate one fifth (20%) of certain annual surplus earnings to the Imam or his representatives.
The obligatory fast observed by Muslims throughout the month of Ramadan, the fourth Pillar of Sunni Islam.
The ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, during which Muslims fast from dawn to sunset; the month in which the Qur'an was first revealed.
Laylat al-Qadr — the night in the last ten days of Ramadan on which the Qur'an was first revealed to Muhammad, regarded as the most blessed night of the year.
